Varicocele repair may improve sperm parameters and fertility in carefully selected patients being evaluated for infertility. A
A varicocele is a dilation of the testicular vein and the pampiniform plexus within the scrotum.

Varicoceles can be categorized as: Grade 1: enlargement of the venous plexus of spermatic tone evident only by palpation during the Valsalva maneuver. Grade 2: enlargement of the venous plexus of spermatic tone evident only by palpation at upright position. Grade 3: enlargement of the venous plexus of spermatic tone is visually evident.
Varicoceles are present in 15% to 20% of healthy adolescent and adult males and in 35 to 40% of men presenting with primary infertility and in up to 80% of men with secondary infertility.
Prevalence is inversely related to BMI.

In 1 study, varicoceles were more common in first-degree relatives of patients with varicoceles than a control group (45.4% vs 11%), especially among brothers (55.1%). In a second similar study, 33.9% of first-degree relatives (36.2% of brothers) versus 12% of controls had varicoceles.

Varicoceles are the most common physical finding in infertile men. However, 80% of varicoceles are not associated with infertility,and indisputable evidence that varicocele repair increases fertility does not exist.

Varicoceles are caused by retrograde blood flow in the internal spermatic vein, resulting in dilation of the pampiniform plexus.

Ninety percent of varicoceles are present on the left. There are fewer right-sided varicoceles because of enhanced drainage of the right testicular vein secondary to its shorter course terminating in an oblique angle of entry into the high flow of the vena cava. The left testicular vein has a longer course and a right-angle entry into the lower flow of the renal vein.

Differential.Differential_Features: Soft mass in the scrotum protruding from the inguinal canal
Smooth scrotal swelling that is typically nontender and transilluminates easily
Smooth, spherical cysts often located on the epididymis
Painful engorgement of the epididymis often associated with dysuria
Painless, firm, irregular mass on the surface of the testis
Abrupt-onset severe pain with "bell clapper" deformity and loss of cremasteric reflex

list.listitem: Most varicoceles are asymptomatic and are found as a nonpainful scrotal mass; 80% to 90% of varicoceles are present on the left side, and they may be bilateral. A small minority of varicoceles will present as an aching pain that is partially or totally relieved by lying down.

Varicoceles are classically described as having the consistency of a "bag of worms," most commonly located above the testis. Varicoceles are more prominent with standing or performing a Valsalva maneuver. They will decompress with the patient supine. Physical examination is moderately sensitive for detecting varicocele (71%-74%).

Grading of varicoceles is based on physical examination. Grade I are small and palpable only with Valsalva maneuver; grade II are easily palpable without a Valsalva maneuver with the patient standing; and grade III are large enough to be detected visually.
Ultrasonography is the test of choice if there is any doubt about the diagnosis of varicocele. In a study of infertile men, it was 97% sensitive and 94% specific (LR+ 16.2, LR– 0.03).
For patients with hypoplasia of the affected testis, consider semen analysis to assess the impact on fertility. Effects can be seen on sperm count, mobility, and morphology.

Some varicoceles are caused by retroperitoneal masses that obstruct the spermatic vein. If a varicocele has a sudden onset, does not reduce in size with the patient supine, or is right sided, imaging with CT or ultrasound of the abdomen and pelvis should be performed to rule out malignancy.

Varicoceles are typically found on asymptomatic patients during routine physical examination or on self-examination. The dilated pampiniform plexus is appreciated with a "bag of worms" finding on physical examination and is almost always on the left.
Varicoceles that present either on the right side or with rapid change warrant further evaluation with pelvic and abdominal ultrasound or CT to rule out malignancy as a cause.

Otherwise, varicoceles are traditionally worked up and treated in infertile couples. Given the lack of evidence that varicocele repair is effective at improving fertility rates, a careful discussion of risks and benefits is essential.
Men who undergo treatment traditionally are infertile with grade II or grade III varicoceles and abnormal sperm parameters. C
Varicocelectomy improves sperm parameters and may improve pregnancy rates. A

Varicocele repair is controversial. It is usually done to correct infertility, so it is performed in the setting of an infertile couple in which the male partner has both an abnormal semen analysis and a grade II or grade III varicocele. Although studies have shown improved semen analysis after repair, meta-analyses show no statistically significant increase in conception rates.

A recent Cochrane review shows there may be some benefit to varicocele repair for fertility, but the evidence base is weak. There is inadequate evidence to determine if radiologic or surgical interventions are superior. A recent RCT showed an improvement in the pregnancy rate with surgery (NNT = 5).

A systematic review of 12 randomized and non-randomized studies with 1357 patients concluded that varicocele treatment improved pregnancy rates, a finding with borderline statistical significance (OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.0 to 1.65, p = 0.048).
One meta-analysis suggested that optimal time for semen parameters post-varicocelectomy may be three months indicating this may be a preferable time for conception.
A systematic review found improvement in sperm parameters (concentration, motility, morphology) but did not report pregnancy outcomes.
NICE states: "men should not be offered surgery for varicoceles as a form of fertility treatment because it does not improve pregnancy rates."

There are 3 main surgical approaches: an open inguinal approach, a laparoscopic approach, and subinguinal microscopic varicocelectomy. There are no statistically significant differences in pregnancy rates between them based on RCTs. One RCT, found that microsurgery compared with either open or laparoscopic techniques had a lower rate of hydrocele (0%, 2.8%, and 5.4%, respectively), fewer recurrences (2.6%, 11%, and 17%, respectively), and resulted in a higher sperm count and motility; pregnancy rates at 1 year were similar.
Two percutaneous methods also exist: a retrograde embolization and anterograde sclerotherapy. These have similar complication rates but higher failure rates than the laparoscopic technique.
A study randomized patients with left grade 3 varicocele to scrotal antegrade sclerotherapy or laparascopie Palomo surgery. Results were similar at 1 year.

The two most common complications of surgery are hydrocele and varicocele recurrence. Depending on surgical technique, hydrocele rates range from 0% to 15.1%. Recurrence rates of varicoceles range from 0% to 9.0%. The lowest incidence of these two complications consistently comes from the group undergoing subinguinal microscopic varicocelectomy.
Other problems include wound complications and scrotal edema. Among the surgical approaches, the laparoscopic technique has a lower incidence of these complications.
Varicocele recurrence rates increase with the size of the varicocele that was initially treated. B
Before a patient undergoes a varicocele repair, engage in a discussion outlining the lack of evidence that such a procedure will improve the chances of conception. C

Treatment is typically considered in adolescents who have grade II or grade III hydroceles and ipsilateral testicular hypotrophy of >2 mL or 20% confirmed by at least 2 measurements taken 12 months apart. In adolescents who have such varicoceles without hypotrophy, yearly measurement of testicular volume is recommended by expert opinion.
Treatment of adolescents has been shown to result in catch-up growth of the affected testicle and improved sperm parameters. However, no data exist concerning improved fertility.

The reason to treat an adolescent would be to maintain fertility. However, 80% of varicoceles are not associated with infertility, and there is a lack of clear evidence that repair of the varicocele improves fertility. Therefore, operating on a teenage boy involves subjecting him to the risk of a surgery that has no proven benefit to fix an abnormality that is unlikely to cause infertility.
Long term outcomes of treatment in children and adolescents are unknown. There is not enough evidence to compare different interventions for short-term outcomes.
